Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others
Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel isolated and set apart from others
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
There is something about me that made the event happen

vignette: Mateo Cruz was fifty-three when the memory still arrived unbidden. It began on a Tuesday evening in a poorly lit municipal parking lot, the kind of routine traffic stop that had never frightened him before, until the officer's hand came down too hard on his shoulder. The confrontation escalated in seconds. Mateo remembered the cold concrete against his cheek, the sharp tear of skin along his jaw, and the suffocating weight of a knee digging into his ribs while he pleaded for air. When it ended, he walked away with a bruised chest, a stitched lip, and the chilling realization that he had been treated as a threat simply for existing in his own neighborhood. He had come to believe that there was something about him that made the event happen-something in his posture, his accent, the way he had spoken-that should have warned him earlier. The guilt settled alongside the physical pain, which lingered in his left side as a persistent, dull ache that flared whenever he leaned forward at his drafting table. The somatic discomfort and the visual reminders became parallel realities during his days as a tax consultant. Long hours spent reviewing complex estate ledgers soon turned into a quiet captivity. His home office, once a place of steady calculation, now required careful navigation. He positioned his chair facing the door, kept his keys on the desk within arm's reach, and rehearsed escape routes whenever a new vendor visited his building. The pain in his ribs would flare during these visits, not as a signal, but as a steady companion to his scanning. He would sit through quarterly reviews, his eyes fixed on the window to track the service elevator, his shoulder tensing at the sound of a keycard. The visual reminders arrived uninvited: a nurse adjusting a client's blood pressure cuff, a colleague wiping a paper cut, a news anchor showing a bruised face during a segment on civil rights. Each image landed with the same weight. He could not look at news clips or hear clients describe arrests without feeling the memory of the victims press against his ribs. The isolation followed quietly; he stopped answering calls from old friends, convinced that his presence only dragged people toward danger. When he did step outside, his neck would crane instinctively over his shoulder. Checking behind him became a rhythm as automatic as his morning coffee-glancing at rearview mirrors, noting footsteps on the pavement, wondering if someone was still following the line of events that had begun in that lot. His professional world contracted accordingly. He could not walk into a space he could not scan for exits or identify threats. Before entering any new building, he would pause at the threshold, mapping the nearest stairwell, the fire exit, the path to his car. He needed to know the way out before he could even cross the threshold. This habit meant he stopped accepting site consultations, citing travel complications, while his own office remained a fortress of familiar sightlines. Clients who expected his expertise found him deflecting meetings to email, his voice growing clipped and distant. His caseload halved over the winter, and his reputation tarnished by no-shows and abrupt cancellations. He was certain that his life was not worth living anymore, a quiet exhaustion that settled in his chest during the long, silent weekends after his divorce. The despair and the physical ache coexisted with the constant scanning, none of it explaining the other. They simply occupied the same days. What frightened him most was not the memory itself, but the certainty that it could be triggered by anything that resembled the conditions of his injury. The ache in his ribs, the sight of a split lip on a newspaper photograph, the sudden silence of a crowded room-all of it converged into a landscape where he could no longer trust his own safety. It was the shrinking of his practice that finally pushed him through the clinic doors. What he was hoping for, he admitted only after several sessions, was not a return to who he had been, but a way to stop bracing for the next blow. He wanted to sit in a room without calculating the exits, to look at his own hands without waiting for the pain to spike, and to finally untangle the memory from the blame. Until then, he would keep checking behind him, carrying the weight of a life that felt both entirely his own and entirely unlivable.
